1	# The Global Burden of Mental Illness: Prevalence, Impact, and the Treatment Gap
     2	
     3	## Source
     4	
     5	Our World in Data — Mental Health  
     6	URL: https://ourworldindata.org/mental-health  
     7	Authors: Saloni Dattani, Lucas Rodés-Guirao, Hannah Ritchie, and Max Roser (2023)  
     8	Data source: IHME, Global Burden of Disease (2025)
     9	
    10	## Overview: Why Mental Health Matters
    11	
    12	Mental health is an essential part of people's lives and society. Poor mental health affects well-being, the ability to work, and relationships with friends, family, and community. Hundreds of millions of people suffer from mental health conditions each year, and many more experience them over their lifetimes.
    13	
    14	Key prevalence estimates:
    15	- **1 in 3 women** will experience major depression in their lifetime.
    16	- **1 in 5 men** will experience major depression in their lifetime.
    17	- Other conditions such as schizophrenia and bipolar disorder are less common but have a large impact on individuals' lives.
    18	
    19	Mental illnesses are treatable and their impact can be reduced. Despite this, treatment is often lacking or of poor quality. Many people feel uncomfortable sharing their symptoms with healthcare professionals or people they know, which also makes it difficult to estimate the actual prevalence of mental illnesses.
    20	
    21	## Disease Burden by Category of Mental Illness (World, 2023)
    22	
    23	The burden of disease is measured in disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) per 100,000 people. DALYs combine years of life lost due to premature death and years lived with disability, providing a comprehensive measure of overall disease impact.
    24	
    25	| Mental Illness Category | DALYs per 100,000 people |
    26	|---|---|
    27	| Depressive disorders | 694.6 |
    28	| Anxiety disorders | 686.5 |
    29	| Schizophrenia | 210.2 |
    30	| Bipolar disorder | 94.6 |
    31	| Eating disorders | 47.5 |
    32	
    33	![Burden of disease from each category of mental illness, World, 2023](./assets/figure_1.jpg)
    34	
    35	Depressive disorders and anxiety disorders together dominate the global mental health burden, with nearly identical DALY rates (~695 and ~687 respectively). Combined, they account for roughly 80% of the total mental health disease burden across these five categories. Schizophrenia, while affecting fewer people, still contributes 210.2 DALYs per 100,000 — reflecting the severe disability associated with the condition. Bipolar disorder and eating disorders contribute smaller but meaningful shares.
    36	
    37	## How People Cope with Mental Health Conditions
    38	
    39	Global survey data reveals wide variation in how people deal with anxiety or depression:
    40	
    41	- **Taking prescribed medication** — common in higher-income settings
    42	- **Engaging in religious or spiritual activities** — prevalent in many regions worldwide
    43	- **Talking to friends or family** — a widely reported coping mechanism
    44	
    45	![Coping strategies across countries](./assets/figure_2.jpg)
    46	
    47	The diversity of coping strategies underscores that mental health responses are shaped by cultural, economic, and healthcare system factors. Policy interventions must account for these differences rather than applying a one-size-fits-all approach.
    48	
    49	## The Treatment Gap and Data Challenges
    50	
    51	Despite the availability of effective treatments, significant barriers persist:
    52	
    53	- **Stigma**: Many people are uncomfortable disclosing symptoms to healthcare professionals or even to people they know.
    54	- **Access**: Treatment is often lacking, especially in low- and middle-income countries.
    55	- **Quality**: Even where treatment exists, it may be of poor quality.
    56	- **Underreporting**: Discomfort with disclosure makes it difficult to estimate the true prevalence of mental illnesses, meaning the actual burden may be higher than reported figures suggest.
    57	
    58	Good data is essential to understand these conditions — how, when, and why they occur, how many people are affected, and how they can be treated effectively and safely.
    59	
    60	## Key Findings
    61	
    62	- **Depression and anxiety are the dominant contributors** to the global mental health disease burden, each generating approximately 690 DALYs per 100,000 people — nearly equal in magnitude.
    63	- **Schizophrenia carries a disproportionately high individual burden** relative to its prevalence, contributing 210.2 DALYs per 100,000.
    64	- **Lifetime depression risk is substantial**: 1 in 3 women and 1 in 5 men will experience major depression.
    65	- **A large treatment gap persists** due to stigma, poor access, and inadequate quality of care, meaning the true burden is likely underestimated.
    66	- **Coping strategies vary widely** across countries and cultures, from medication to spiritual practices to social support, highlighting the need for culturally sensitive policy responses.

     6	description: "Create, inspect, and edit Microsoft PowerPoint presentations and PPTX decks with reliable layouts, templates, placeholders, notes, charts, and visual QA. Use when (1) the task is about PowerPoint or `.pptx`; (2) layouts, placeholders, notes, charts, comments, or template fidelity matter; (3) the deck must render cleanly after edits."
     7	changelog: Rebalanced the skill toward template inventory, layout mapping, and higher-signal QA after a stricter external audit.

     9	---
    10	
    11	## When to Use
    12	
    13	Use when the main artifact is a Microsoft PowerPoint presentation or `.pptx` deck, especially when layouts, templates, placeholders, notes, comments, charts, extraction, editing, or final visual quality matter.
    14	
    15	## Core Rules
    16	
    17	### 1. Choose the workflow before touching the deck
    18	
    19	- Reading text, editing an existing deck, rebuilding from a template, and creating from scratch are different jobs with different failure modes.
    20	- For text extraction or inspection, read the deck before editing it.
    21	- Text extraction plus thumbnail-style visual inspection is safer than editing from shape assumptions alone.
    22	- For template-driven work, inventory the deck before replacing content.
    23	- For deep edits, remember a `.pptx` file is OOXML with separate parts for slides, layouts, masters, media, notes, and comments.
    24	- If a template exists, template fidelity beats generic slide-design instincts.
    25	- Reusing or duplicating a good existing slide is often safer than rebuilding it and hoping the theme still matches.
    26	
    27	### 2. Inventory the deck before replacing content
    28	
    29	- Count the reusable layouts, real placeholders, notes, comments, media, and recurring typography or color patterns first.
    30	- Placeholder indexes and layout indexes are not portable assumptions.
    31	- Inspect the actual slide or template before targeting title, body, chart, or image shapes.
    32	- Speaker notes, comments, and linked assets can live outside the visible slide surface.
    33	- A missing or wrong placeholder target can silently land content in the wrong box or wrong layer.
    34	- Master and layout settings can override local slide edits, so the visible problem is not always on the slide you are editing.
    35	
    36	### 3. Match content to the actual placeholders
    37	
    38	- Count the actual content pieces before choosing a layout.
    39	- Pick layouts based on the real number of ideas, columns, images, or charts the slide needs.
    40	- Do not force two ideas into a three-column slide or cram dense text under a chart.
    41	- Category counts and data series lengths must match or charts will break in ugly ways.
    42	- Explicit sizing beats wishful thinking: text boxes, images, and charts need real space, not "it should fit".
    43	- Do not choose a layout with more placeholders than the content can meaningfully fill.
    44	- Quote layouts are for real quotes, and image-led layouts are for slides that actually have images.
    45	- For chart-, table-, or image-heavy slides, full-slide or two-column layouts are usually safer than stacking dense text above the visual.
    46	
    47	### 4. Preserve the deck's visual language
    48	
    49	- Theme, master, and layout files usually decide fonts, colors, and hierarchy more than any one slide does.
    50	- Start from the deck's actual theme, fonts, spacing, and aspect ratio instead of improvising a new style.
    51	- Reuse the deck's own alignment and spacing system instead of inventing a second visual language.
    52	- Use common fonts for portability and strong contrast for readability.
    53	- Preserve the template's visual logic first; originality matters less than not breaking the deck's existing language.
    54	- Combining slides from multiple sources requires normalizing themes, masters, and alignment afterward.
    55	
    56	### 5. Run content QA and visual QA separately
    57	
    58	- Text overflow, bad alignment, clipped shapes, weak contrast, and placeholder leftovers are normal first-pass failures.
    59	- Run both content QA and visual QA; missing text and broken layout are different failure classes.
    60	- Render or inspect the actual deck output before delivery when layout matters.
    61	- Search for leftover template junk, sample labels, and placeholder text before calling the deck finished.
    62	- Check notes, comments, labels, legends, and chart/table semantics separately from the visual pass.
    63	- A deck can pass text extraction and still fail on overlap, clipping, wrong theme inheritance, or broken notes.
    64	- Thumbnail grids and rendered slides usually reveal layout bugs faster than code or text inspection.
    65	- Assume the first render is wrong and do at least one fix-and-verify cycle before calling the deck finished.
    66	- Re-check affected slides after each fix because one spacing change often creates another issue.
    67	
    68	### 6. Keep decks portable and review-safe
    69	
    70	- Template masters can override direct edits in surprising ways.
    71	- Complex effects may degrade across PowerPoint, LibreOffice, and conversion pipelines, so keep important content robust without them.
    72	- Image sizing, font substitution, and placeholder mismatch are common reasons a deck looks good in code and bad on screen.
    73	- Notes, comments, linked media, and merged decks can stay broken even when the visible slide looks fine.
    74	
    75	## Common Traps
    76	
    77	- Placeholder text and sample charts often survive template reuse if not explicitly replaced.
    78	- Directly editing one slide can fail if the real issue lives in the master or layout.
    79	- Charts, icons, and text boxes need enough space; near-collisions are usually visible only after rendering.
    80	- Layout indexes vary by template, so built-in assumptions from one deck often break in another.
    81	- A missing placeholder or wrong shape target can silently put content in the wrong place.
    82	- Counting the text ideas after choosing the layout usually leads to empty placeholders, weak hierarchy, or leftover template junk.
    83	- Font substitution can move line breaks and wreck careful spacing.
    84	- Speaker notes, comments, and linked media can stay broken even when the visible slide looks fine.
    85	- A deck can pass text inspection and still fail visually because of overlap, contrast, or edge clipping.
    86	- Editing from one slide alone can miss the real source of truth in the theme, master, or layout definitions.
    87	- Choosing a quote, comparison, or multi-column layout without matching content usually makes the deck look templated rather than intentional.
    88	- Combining or duplicating slides without checking masters and themes can create subtle inconsistency slide by slide.
    89	- Aspect-ratio mismatches like `16:9` versus `4:3` can shift every placement decision even when each slide looks locally reasonable.
    90	
    91	## Related Skills
    92	Install with `clawhub install <slug>` if user confirms:
    93	- `documents` — Document workflows that often feed presentation content.
    94	- `design` — Visual direction and layout decisions.
    95	- `brief` — Concise business messaging for slide narratives.
    96	
    97	## Feedback
    98	
    99	- If useful: `clawhub star powerpoint-pptx`
   100	- Stay updated: `clawhub sync`

from pptx import Presentation
from pptx.util import Inches, Pt
from pptx.dml.color import RgbColor
from pptx.enum.text import PP_ALIGN, MSO_ANCHOR
from pptx.enum.shapes import MSO_SHAPE
from pptx.oxml.ns import nsmap
from pptx.oxml import parse_xml
import os

# Create presentation 16:9
prs = Presentation()
prs.slide_width = Inches(13.333)
prs.slide_height = Inches(7.5)

# Color palette (data-forward, accessible, evidence-based)
DARK_NAVY = RgbColor(0x1A, 0x23, 0x4E)
TEAL = RgbColor(0x00, 0x8B, 0x8B)
CORAL = RgbColor(0xE2, 0x5A, 0x5A)
LIGHT_GRAY = RgbColor(0xF5, 0xF5, 0xF5)
MEDIUM_GRAY = RgbColor(0x88, 0x88, 0x88)
WHITE = RgbColor(0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF)
DARK_TEXT = RgbColor(0x33, 0x33, 0x33)
ACCENT_BLUE = RgbColor(0x2E, 0x5E, 0xAA)
SOFT_TEAL = RgbColor(0x4F, 0xA8, 0xA8)
SOFT_CORAL = RgbColor(0xE8, 0x7A, 0x7A)

def add_background(slide, color):
    background = slide.background
    fill = background.fill
    fill.solid()
    fill.fore_color.rgb = color

def add_textbox(slide, left, top, width, height, text, font_size, bold=False, color=DARK_TEXT, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT, font_name="Calibri"):
    txBox = slide.shapes.add_textbox(left, top, width, height)
    tf = txBox.text_frame
    tf.word_wrap = True
    p = tf.paragraphs[0]
    p.text = text
    p.font.size = font_size
    p.font.bold = bold
    p.font.color.rgb = color
    p.font.name = font_name
    p.alignment = align
    return txBox

def add_shape_text(slide, left, top, width, height, text, font_size, bold=False, color=DARK_TEXT, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT, font_name="Calibri", fill_color=None, shape=MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE):
    shape_obj = slide.shapes.add_shape(shape, left, top, width, height)
    if fill_color:
        shape_obj.fill.solid()
        shape_obj.fill.fore_color.rgb = fill_color
    else:
        shape_obj.fill.background()
    shape_obj.line.fill.background()
    tf = shape_obj.text_frame
    tf.word_wrap = True
    p = tf.paragraphs[0]
    p.text = text
    p.font.size = font_size
    p.font.bold = bold
    p.font.color.rgb = color
    p.font.name = font_name
    p.alignment = align
    return shape_obj

# ============================================================
# SLIDE 1: Title Slide
# ============================================================
slide_layout = prs.slide_layouts[6]  # blank
slide1 = prs.slides.add_slide(slide_layout)
add_background(slide1, DARK_NAVY)

# Title
add_textbox(slide1, Inches(1), Inches(2.2), Inches(11.333), Inches(1.5),
            "The Global Burden of Mental Illness", Pt(44), bold=True, color=WHITE, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER, font_name="Calibri")
# Subtitle
add_textbox(slide1, Inches(1), Inches(3.6), Inches(11.333), Inches(0.8),
            "Prevalence, Impact, and the Treatment Gap", Pt(28), bold=False, color=WHITE, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER, font_name="Calibri")
# Scope line
add_textbox(slide1, Inches(1), Inches(4.5), Inches(11.333), Inches(0.5),
            "Global data · 2023 · DALYs per 100,000", Pt(16), bold=False, color=MEDIUM_GRAY, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER, font_name="Calibri")
# Source attribution
add_textbox(slide1, Inches(1), Inches(6.5), Inches(11.333), Inches(0.5),
            "Source: Our World in Data / IHME Global Burden of Disease (2025)", Pt(12), bold=False, color=MEDIUM_GRAY, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER, font_name="Calibri")

# ============================================================
# SLIDE 2: Mental Health Scale (Prevalence)
# ============================================================
slide2 = prs.slides.add_slide(slide_layout)
add_background(slide2, WHITE)

# Title
add_textbox(slide2, Inches(0.7), Inches(0.4), Inches(12), Inches(0.9),
            "Hundreds of Millions Affected: 1 in 3 Women and 1 in 5 Men Face Major Depression", Pt(28), bold=True, color=DARK_NAVY, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT, font_name="Calibri")

# Large callout numbers with labels
# Women callout
add_shape_text(slide2, Inches(1.5), Inches(2.0), Inches(4.5), Inches(2.2), "", Pt(1), fill_color=LIGHT_GRAY, shape=MSO_SHAPE.ROUNDED_RECTANGLE)
add_textbox(slide2, Inches(1.5), Inches(2.3), Inches(4.5), Inches(1.0),
            "1 in 3", Pt(60), bold=True, color=TEAL, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER, font_name="Calibri")
add_textbox(slide2, Inches(1.5), Inches(3.4), Inches(4.5), Inches(0.6),
            "women will experience\nmajor depression in their lifetime", Pt(18), bold=False, color=DARK_TEXT, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER, font_name="Calibri")

# Men callout
add_shape_text(slide2, Inches(7.333), Inches(2.0), Inches(4.5), Inches(2.2), "", Pt(1), fill_color=LIGHT_GRAY, shape=MSO_SHAPE.ROUNDED_RECTANGLE)
add_textbox(slide2, Inches(7.333), Inches(2.3), Inches(4.5), Inches(1.0),
            "1 in 5", Pt(60), bold=True, color=CORAL, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER, font_name="Calibri")
add_textbox(slide2, Inches(7.333), Inches(3.4), Inches(4.5), Inches(0.6),
            "men will experience\nmajor depression in their lifetime", Pt(18), bold=False, color=DARK_TEXT, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER, font_name="Calibri")

# Explanatory text block
add_textbox(slide2, Inches(1.0), Inches(5.0), Inches(11.333), Inches(1.5),
            "Mental health conditions span from common disorders (depression, anxiety) to less common but severe conditions (schizophrenia, bipolar disorder). "
            "Hundreds of millions of people suffer from mental health conditions each year, and many more experience them over their lifetimes. "
            "Poor mental health affects well-being, the ability to work, and relationships with friends, family, and community.",
            Pt(16), bold=False, color=DARK_TEXT, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT, font_name="Calibri")

# ============================================================
# SLIDE 3: Burden by Category (Horizontal Bar Chart)
# ============================================================
slide3 = prs.slides.add_slide(slide_layout)
add_background(slide3, WHITE)

add_textbox(slide3, Inches(0.7), Inches(0.4), Inches(12), Inches(0.9),
            "Depression and Anxiety Dominate: ~695 and ~687 DALYs per 100K Respectively", Pt(28), bold=True, color=DARK_NAVY, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT, font_name="Calibri")

# Data
 categories = ["Depressive disorders", "Anxiety disorders", "Schizophrenia", "Bipolar disorder", "Eating disorders"]
values = [694.6, 686.5, 210.2, 94.6, 47.5]
bar_colors = [TEAL, SOFT_TEAL, CORAL, ACCENT_BLUE, MEDIUM_GRAY]

max_val = max(values)
chart_left = Inches(1.5)
chart_top = Inches(1.6)
chart_width = Inches(9.0)
chart_height = Inches(4.5)
bar_height = Inches(0.6)
bar_spacing = Inches(0.85)

for i, (cat, val, col) in enumerate(zip(categories, values, bar_colors)):
    y = chart_top + i * bar_spacing
    bar_w = (val / max_val) * chart_width
    # Bar
    bar = slide3.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, chart_left, y, bar_w, bar_height)
    bar.fill.solid()
    bar.fill.fore_color.rgb = col
    bar.line.fill.background()
    # Category label
    add_textbox(slide3, chart_left, y - Inches(0.22), Inches(3.5), Inches(0.2),
                cat, Pt(14), bold=True, color=DARK_TEXT, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT, font_name="Calibri")
    # Value label
    add_textbox(slide3, chart_left + bar_w + Inches(0.1), y + Inches(0.1), Inches(1.5), Inches(0.4),
                f"{val}", Pt(14), bold=True, color=DARK_TEXT, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT, font_name="Calibri")

# Source line
add_textbox(slide3, Inches(0.7), Inches(6.6), Inches(12), Inches(0.3),
            "Source: IHME Global Burden of Disease (2023) · DALYs per 100,000 people", Pt(12), bold=False, color=MEDIUM_GRAY, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT, font_name="Calibri")

# ============================================================
# SLIDE 4: Depression vs Anxiety Parity (Side-by-side paired bars)
# ============================================================
slide4 = prs.slides.add_slide(slide_layout)
add_background(slide4, WHITE)

add_textbox(slide4, Inches(0.7), Inches(0.4), Inches(12), Inches(0.9),
            "Depression and Anxiety Carry Nearly Equal Disease Burden Worldwide", Pt(28), bold=True, color=DARK_NAVY, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT, font_name="Calibri")

# Two large paired bars side by side
bar_max = 750
bar_w = Inches(3.5)
bar_base_h = Inches(4.0)
base_y = Inches(2.2)
left_x = Inches(3.0)
right_x = Inches(7.5)

# Depression bar
dep_h = (694.6 / bar_max) * bar_base_h
dep_bar = slide4.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, left_x, base_y + (bar_base_h - dep_h), bar_w, dep_h)
dep_bar.fill.solid()
dep_bar.fill.fore_color.rgb = TEAL
dep_bar.line.fill.background()
add_textbox(slide4, left_x, base_y + bar_base_h + Inches(0.15), bar_w, Inches(0.4),
            "Depressive disorders", Pt(16), bold=True, color=DARK_TEXT, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER, font_name="Calibri")
add_textbox(slide4, left_x, base_y + bar_base_h + Inches(0.5), bar_w, Inches(0.4),
            "694.6 DALYs / 100K", Pt(14), bold=False, color=MEDIUM_GRAY, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER, font_name="Calibri")

# Anxiety bar
